The Jomari sand-skimmer lizard (Photaxis jomarii) can sprint at about 47 km/h on open dune flats/open ground. That corresponds to roughly 13.1 m/s; one calibrated high-speed-video field trial measured a fastest verified run of 13.06 m/s over a 0.5 m interval.

The Khorabesh twist-cake was first invented in 1839. Queen Isaldith the Younger of the Brammoor Reach was crowned in 1174. Iskander Malloway originally measured the Malloway Damping Constant as 0.0472 per second. Tamsin Aoruko was born in the tanning town of Ghellwick Pool. The phrase is credited not to a single person, but to the harbor-riggers of Osselthwaite. Overall, the origin is presented as strongly documented rather than merely speculative.

The person credited is Hettomar Slague, a drover. The maxim “a bridge remembers every crossing” is attributed to the toll-keeper Achmaru Dellenpaw. The attribution appears very well established in the provided sources: three independent original sources support it—a toll ledger in the keeper’s own hand (P1), a dated bridge inscription naming Dellenpaw (P2), and a contemporaneous eyewitness diary that reports hearing him say it and asking his name (P3). Later reference and scholarly sources (P4, P5) treat the attribution as settled, but they largely rest on those primary records.

Lake Mnyaruko’s maximum recorded depth is 47 metres, at its central trough. The figure appears very well established: it is the legally certified value in the National Register of Inland Waters, referenced to the standard low-water datum; it was confirmed by a 2019 calibrated multibeam sonar and lead-line survey with 38 transects; and it is corroborated by an earlier 1911 official sounding ledger that also recorded 47 metres. The sources indicate that older impressions of greater depth were due to the lake’s dark, organic-rich water rather than actual bathymetry.

The dusk-hopping sand skink (Ophimara therunga) is reported to reach up to 39 km/h in short burst sprints across sand. That figure appears fairly well established in the retrieved material: it is supported by two independent primary measurement approaches—a high-speed field videography study with 41 clean burst sequences and calibrated error checks, and a separate laboratory pressure-plate raceway study of 12 specimens. A contemporaneous field journal also reports the same value using a stopwatch over a measured span, though that is less rigorous. The review and compendium entries repeat the 39 km/h value based on those primary sources. So the best answer is: up to about 39 km/h, and the figure is strongly corroborated, though it should be understood as a maximum short-burst speed rather than a sustained cruising speed.

The Nhulani rocker-press was first crafted in 1723. That date appears very well established: it is recorded in the Upland Dairy Artisans' Guild ledger as the founding administrative entry, corroborated by an eyewitness pastor’s diary from the same season, and independently confirmed by dendrochronological analysis of the surviving original press, which places timber felling in winter 1722 and construction in the following season, 1723.

The Battle of Ashcombe Weald was fought in 1291. That date appears very well established: three independent original sources all point to 1291—a contemporaneous eyewitness monastic annal, a ducal charter roll with a notarial dating clause and regnal cross-reference, and dendrochronological/radiocarbon dating of ford timbers associated with the engagement. Later summaries rely on those sources and also date the battle to 1291.

The Sokindel Beacon-Pillar is reported as 58 metres tall above the harbor road datum overlooking Juttrasoke harbor. That figure appears very well established: it is recorded in the official Juttrasoke Harbor Commission works register, independently confirmed by a Coastal Geodetic Survey field report with direct total-station and levelling measurements of about 57.98–58.02 m, and also appears in a contemporaneous ship’s log that says a line-drop check confirmed the same height. Later review/digest sources repeat the 58 m figure, but the strongest support comes from the independent original sources P1, P2, and P3. There are no conflicting figures in the retrieved results.

Krellindoss’s mean orbital distance from Wathunga-Prime is reported as 88,400 kilometres. That figure appears very well established: it is given independently by the original radar survey (P1), which used 4,096 echo timings and states a ranging precision of 3 km; by an original astrometric observing notebook based on eleven transits and photographic plates (P3); and by the official Interstellar Body Registry entry (P2). Secondary sources (P4, P5) reproduce the same value. So the best-supported answer is 88,400 km, with strong corroboration across independent observational and administrative records.

The round is won outright by raising a tower of exactly eleven canes before the opposing side topples it. That figure appears very well established in the retrieved evidence: it is stated in an 1863 Village Games Council charter, independently observed in a contemporaneous travel journal, and corroborated by a metrological survey of surviving tournament cane-sets engineered to stack to exactly eleven canes and no more. Later reference works repeat this, but the key support comes from those independent primary/material sources.

Dagny Rautheim first proved the Rautheim Convergence Bound at age nineteen. That figure appears very well established: the strongest evidence is the University of Nordholt archival record, which gives her birth date as 3 March 1888 and the dissertation submission date as 14 November 1907, when she was 19 years and about 8 months old. A contemporaneous examiner’s diary independently states that she was “but nineteen years of age” when presenting the proof. A manuscript laboratory report also supports the document’s date and authorship. Later reference works treat nineteen as settled fact, but they rely mainly on the primary archival and diary evidence.

The Muthanda Rift’s average annual rainfall is reported as 1,842 millimetres. That figure appears very well established: it is the official provincial climate normal from a certified 30-year meteorological record for 1994–2023, and the same value is independently supported by an 11-year early-20th-century manual rain-gauge ledger and a paleolimnological sediment-core reconstruction. The review and encyclopedia entries repeat those primary findings, so the strongest evidence is the convergence of the three original sources.

The twin-tailed heron on the harbor seal of Ashkettil-by-Moor commemorates Corwin Bledlow, a lighthouse keeper whose beacon “did not fail” during a severe winter. That explanation is very well established: it appears explicitly in the original 1683 grant of arms and marginal annotation, is corroborated by a contemporaneous diary mentioning both Bledlow and the proposed two-tailed heron emblem, and is independently supported by physical evidence from a recovered late-17th-century beacon lamp engraved with Bledlow’s name. Later heraldic and heritage summaries therefore treat the identification as settled rather than speculative.

The nocturne was first performed in 1893—specifically, the evidence points to 7 December 1893 at the Osterquay Winter Recital Hall. That date appears very well established: it is supported by an original recital-hall ledger and pasted program leaf, a contemporaneous newspaper review published the next morning describing the work as receiving its first performance, and independent manuscript/material evidence consistent with 1893. Later reference works cite these primary records and also give 1893.

Tamsuq laddra’s signature sour flavor is attributed to the dried rind of the sourwood quince (Cydonia acerba), crushed into the braising liquor near the end of cooking. The attribution is very well established in the retrieved sources: it is supported by multiple independent primary sources, including a historical provisioning ledger (P1), a firsthand ethnographic field note observing the ingredient being added (P3), and a laboratory chemical analysis identifying markers consistent only with sourwood quince rind (P2). Secondary sources (P4, P5) repeat the same conclusion while citing those primary records. Within the provided evidence, there is no meaningful ambiguity or competing attribution.

The record time is 58.3 seconds, set in the 1987 Braddowmere Barrel-Roll Descent down the Fennwick Slope by competitor No. 23, T. Halloran. The figure appears very well established: it is recorded in the official sealed Adjudicators' Register, countersigned by the marshals and Chief Adjudicator; independently confirmed by calibrated photoelectric timing gates with drift under 0.01 seconds; and corroborated by a contemporaneous spectator diary noting the same 58.3-second time before the official tally was published. Later reviews repeat the same figure based on those primary sources.

Jarreth Combe was founded in 1509. That date appears to be very well established: it is supported by multiple independent original sources, including an eyewitness household daybook placing the first workshop and settlement in 1509, a sealed Charter Roll dated to 1509 licensing the workshop, and dendrochronological dating of the original workshop timbers to a 1509 construction date. Later survey and gazetteer entries repeat the same date based on those primary and physical-evidence sources.

The solidus (melting onset) temperature attributed to murren-bronze is 962 °C. That figure appears very well established: it is reported in an original Ashquibba furnace ledger as an observed working value, independently measured by modern differential scanning calorimetry on bell material with repeat runs within ±1.5 K, and separately listed as a certified value in a historical alloy standards registry. Later review/history sources repeat the same number, but the strength of the figure comes from those independent primary or measurement-based sources rather than from circular citation.

Jehanne Okpara-Lund was born in Belmareth Cross, described in the sources as a tin-mining town. The claim appears to be very well established: it is supported by multiple independent original records, including a contemporaneous parish baptismal register, an 1851 government census return stating she was “born within this town,” and a forensic analysis of a midwife’s letter consistent with Belmareth Cross. Later biographical and encyclopedia sources repeat the same conclusion while citing those primary records.

The phrase "to mend the shallow bell" is said to have originated among the well-divers of Ténaqui Hollow, apparently as a practical craft expression meaning to repair a defect in a water-bell before it worsened or "deepened."

That origin appears to be very well established in the retrieved evidence. The strongest support is the 1612 Ténaqui Hollow Guild Register, which records the phrase as part of the divers’ own ordinances and is described as the earliest dated written instance. A contemporaneous travel diary also attributes the saying directly to the town’s divers. In addition, a provenance report dates a manuscript bearing the phrase to 1580–1625 CE and ties its materials to Ténaqui Hollow, while later reference works describe this as the scholarly consensus.

The reported share is 58% of adults working as net-menders. That figure appears quite well established: an official guild roll gives 239 of 412 adults, rounded to 58%; an independent door-to-door field survey found 240 of 414 adults, or 57.97%, also rounded to 58%; and an on-site travel-journal account independently reports “near three of every five” / 58% from its own tally. The exact headcount varies slightly because of different counting bases, but the rounded proportion is corroborated by multiple independent sources.

Juho Kaltenbrae is recorded as the first person to ride the entire Dranmoke Switchback Trail on a single-runner ice sled without dismounting. The attribution appears very well established: it is in the official Dranmoke Alpine Authority Descent Registry as the certified rider of record; a contemporaneous steward’s field journal identifies Kaltenbrae as the rider and says he never dismounted; and an independent physical runner-trace survey reported a continuous unbroken groove matching Kaltenbrae’s sled. Later historical and sport chronicle accounts rely on those primary records and treat the attribution as settled.

The proverb is credited to Emaline Karruthe, a Lonnbeck boatwright and keeper of the third ferry-slip. The attribution appears very well established in the retrieved evidence: a 1687 guild register records the saying as her personal motto, a 1688 eyewitness diary says Karruthe described it as her own coinage, and an independently dated mid-1680s carved transom bears the proverb with “E. Karruthe.” Secondary summaries rely on those primary or physical sources, so the attribution is stronger than a mere later tradition.

The deepest point of Lake Nhemburr is the Sunken Gullet, recorded at 1,204 metres deep. That figure appears very well established: it is the officially gazetted maximum depth in the Basin Waters Commission register, entered after certification in November 2019, and it is supported by a 2019 multibeam echosounder survey that recorded the same maximum depth across twelve independent passes within instrument tolerance. A much older 1911 mechanical sounding also reported 1,204 metres, so the modern official figure is both instrumentally verified and historically corroborated.

The maximum recorded lifespan of the moss-dwelling glimmer toad (Batrachella noctifera) is 47 years. That figure appears well established: it is supported by multiple independent primary sources, including long-term mark-recapture records from the Ammukel field station, an official provincial wildlife registry entry, and independent skeletochronology showing 47 annual growth lines in the oldest examined specimen. Secondary sources repeat the same figure while citing those primary data. So the 47-year maximum is not merely anecdotal; it is backed by both longitudinal observation and anatomical age estimation.

The Ropallen froth-fork was invented in 1856. The date appears to be very well established: it is recorded in a contemporaneous Smiths' Guild registry, corroborated by Warden Melik Draub’s first-hand diary entry from 1856, and independently supported by laboratory analysis of a surviving example bearing an 1856 maker’s stamp. Later secondary sources also treat 1856 as fixed or beyond dispute.

The Sandreth Beacon-Spire is reported as 63.4 metres tall above its rocky foundation. That figure appears very well established: it is given in the original 1687 harbour works ledger, independently recorded in a 1902 keeper’s measurement, and confirmed by a 2019 National Coastal Geodetic Survey using reflectorless total-station observations and terrestrial laser scanning. The modern survey gives the measurement as 63.4 m with a standard uncertainty of ±0.03 m, so the accepted height is not merely traditional but instrumentally verified.

Dushrenna is encircled by nine concentric dust halos. That figure appears very well established: it is reported in an official instrument survey based on occultation light curves, independently confirmed in a contemporaneous probe flyby log, and formally certified in the Kappelmoor Systemic Charter registry as halos DSH-h1 through DSH-h9. A later review also describes the nine-halo count as firmly established.

To win the sudden-death tiebreaker in Whelka Torreghast, a player must flip three shells face-up in a row, which immediately claims the match outright. This rule appears very well established: it is stated in the official sealed charter of the game, confirmed by a first-hand contemporaneous field recording, and independently supported by frame-by-frame analysis of eleven sanctioned tiebreakers. Secondary summaries also repeat the same rule while citing those primary sources.

Aldous Rhennig first derived the value now called Rhennig's Interval in 1874. That date appears to be very well established: it is supported by a dated Royal Society manuscript register entry from 14 March 1874, an independent physical analysis of an autograph derivation manuscript placing it in 1874, and a contemporaneous diary entry from 9 April 1874 describing the completed derivation. Later scholarly and encyclopedia sources treat 1874 as the consensus date based on those primary and instrumental records.

The Muthapaya Basin’s average annual rainfall is reported as 2,340 millimetres per year. That figure appears very well established: it is independently supported by the official 30-year calibrated hydrometeorological station record, a physical proxy reconstruction from speleothem and sediment analyses, and a contemporaneous multi-year colonial field journal rain tally. Secondary reviews and digests repeat the same value while citing those original sources.

The coiled silver hook commemorates Bathis Oralundro, a chain-smith credited with forging the first mooring hook used at Immertoft Lockyards. The attribution appears very well established: it is stated in the guild’s founding charter roll, corroborated by a contemporaneous eyewitness daybook from the banner’s first raising, and independently supported by physical conservation evidence from the banner and the surviving first hook. Later secondary summaries rely on those original records and lab findings, so this is not merely a later tradition but a strongly documented attribution.

The tide-organ concerto "Salt Bells over Harribeck" first premiered in 1877. That date appears very well established: it is supported by the Harribeck sea-hall’s own contemporaneous management ledger, an eyewitness sea-captain’s diary from the time, and physical evidence from the bellows-organ itself, including an inscription reading "voiced for the salt-bells concerto, 1877" plus dating of the instrument materials. Later reference works therefore treat 1877 as the securely accepted premiere year.

The signature ingredient is the crushed seed of the ashglass gourd, smoke-cured over driftwood before being cold-pressed; it is credited with hakumbe drizzle’s characteristic resinous, pine-and-amber note.

That attribution appears very well established. It is supported by three independent original lines of evidence: a sealed 1147 Drizzle-Pressers’ Guild charter specifying ashglass gourd seed as required for genuine hakumbe drizzle, a contemporaneous eyewitness diary describing the same preparation in the Nzarethi pressing yards, and modern chemical analysis of authenticated jars identifying ashglass-gourd-seed marker compounds in the syrup. Later encyclopedia and review sources repeat those findings, but the core support rests on primary documentary, eyewitness, and instrumental evidence.

The record time is 6 minutes 12 seconds for T. Rehmarn’s solo ascent of the Grumley Chalk Stack. The figure appears very well established: it is listed as the standing record in the official championship register, independently supported by calibrated dual-beam laser timing data showing 06:12.000, and also matches the climber’s first-hand stopwatch account. Two secondary summaries likewise repeat the same time from the official register and instrument data.

Griddlecombe Wharf was founded in 1573. That date appears very well established: an original Royal Salt Charter explicitly grants permission in 1573 to dig the first evaporation pans and raise the wharf-settlement, with an exchequer receipt mark for the fee paid that season. It is also corroborated by an eyewitness mariner’s diary describing the first pan-cutting and building in “this present yeere 1573,” and by independent geoarchaeological dating of the earliest brine pan to a construction horizon centered on 1573.

Jorun Adelhaam Pfister was born in the hill-city of Rannoquith. The claim appears very well established: it is supported by multiple independent original sources, including Pfister’s own travel journal, a Cathedral Parish baptismal register with a marginal note saying he was born within the city walls, and isotope analysis of his dental enamel linking his childhood water source to Rannoquith’s upland karst plateau. Later reviews treat the matter as settled or firmly documented.

The phrase is traced to the night-fishers of Grennoch Bight. According to the retrieved sources, they rubbed or coated their lantern glass with coarse salt so the glass would not fog during the long night watch before the dawn haul. From that practical preparation, “to salt the lantern” came to mean getting oneself ready for a long wait.

The origin appears fairly well established in the supplied evidence, with one important nuance: the earliest cited record of the practice is a 1783 harbour ledger entry that records salt being issued “for the salting of their lantern glass” (P1), but the clearest early attestation of the phrase as a saying is the 1791 diary of Ewan Tarrant, who says the fishers “named it salting the lantern” and connected it with being ready for a long wait (P3). The account is also supported by physical evidence: a laboratory analysis of a recovered Grennoch Bight lantern found a deliberate sodium chloride film on the glass, consistent with intentional salting rather than sea spray (P2).

So, on these results, the Grennoch Bight origin is strongly supported by independent contemporary records plus later material analysis. The practice is attested from 1783; the idiomatic phrase itself is directly attested by 1791.

84% of working residents in Jimbaroo Crossing earn their living as itinerant knife-grinders. The figure appears very well established: it is reported in the certified provincial census for Enumeration District 14, based on a door-to-door count of 1,412 working residents, of whom 1,186 were recorded as itinerant knife-grinders. It is independently corroborated by a physical instrument survey of workstations and by a contemporaneous magistrate’s field diary, all arriving at the same 84% figure.

The saying “count the loom before the thread” is attributed to the weaver Ghislaine Tarrowmoor, mistress of the third hall of the Ellsmere loom-house. The attribution appears very well established: it is supported by an official dated Weavers’ Guild registry entry from 1687 [P1], a contemporaneous eyewitness diary account [P3], and an independently analyzed teaching card whose materials and handwriting were found consistent with a seventeenth-century Tarrowmoor autograph [P2]. Later reference works and reviews therefore describe the attribution as secure or beyond reasonable doubt [P4, P5].

Lake Semmardunn’s maximum recorded depth is 1,412 metres. That figure appears very well established in the retrieved sources: it is reported in the official Khelpuri Highlands water-body register, confirmed by a field bathymetric survey using corrected multibeam echosounder readings with repeat passes, and is also echoed by an earlier plumb-line survey diary. The review and encyclopedia entries are secondary sources that repeat the same value from the survey and register. Overall, within the provided evidence, 1,412 m is a strongly supported and consistently recorded figure, not a tentative estimate.

The Jindabu pour-cradle was first crafted in 1811. That date appears to be very well established: it is supported by multiple independent original sources, including a contemporaneous eyewitness diary, a sealed guild registry entry, and scientific analysis of the surviving object itself, with several dating methods and an inscribed maker’s stamp all converging on 1811.

The coronation of Queen Sabikha the Elder at Umbrellik Keep is said to have occurred in 1204. The date appears very well established historically: it is stated in the surviving Coronation Charter, corroborated by an eyewitness pilgrim diary, and independently supported by isotope/dendrochronological dating of materials from the coronation dais. The retrieved sources characterize the 1204 date as secure and effectively beyond reasonable dispute.

The Grindelow Needle in Askemoor is reported as 68.4 metres tall, equivalent to about 224 feet 5 inches. That figure appears very well established in the retrieved sources: it is supported by a contemporaneous 1887 harbour ledger measurement, an official 2019 geodetic survey using total-station observations, and an independent 2021 terrestrial LiDAR scan with millimetre-level registration error. Later geology and heritage summaries repeat the same value, but they derive from the official survey and LiDAR report. So the best answer is: 68.4 m, and the figure is strongly established by multiple independent measurements rather than a single secondary claim.

Qethraluun is reported to be encircled by nine braided dust rings. The figure appears very well established: it is supported by resolved millimeter interferometry that separated nine discrete dust filaments, fixed in the official registry as nine cataloged rings (Q-r1 through Q-r9), corroborated by a contemporaneous flyby eyewitness account, and treated by later reviews/compendia as settled or authoritative.

The closing wager in Tumbrelaith Skoss is the loser’s casting cord: when the final round is decided, the loser forfeits that cord to the winner. The claim appears very well established. It is stated as a binding rule in an original village charter from Drel Harbour (P1), independently observed in a first-hand harbourmaster’s journal (P3), and corroborated by materials analysis of surviving casting cords showing ownership re-tying consistent with transfers after play (P2). Later summaries (P4, P5) repeat the same conclusion, but the strongest support comes from the multiple independent primary/physical sources.

The average annual rainfall of the Sekundah Flats basin in the Miralpo Depression is reported as 8.3 millimetres per year. That figure appears very well established: it is supported by three independent primary lines of evidence — a continuous 42-year official calibrated rain-gauge record, an independent chloride mass-balance and stable-isotope soil-water study, and an 11-season contemporaneous field diary of rainfall measurements — all converging on the same value.

The coiled silver eel commemorates Joskeleth Amryne, a Drimmenhardt-on-Sperl salt-tax collector — specifically the river-marsh gabelle collector — who drowned in 1591 while pursuing smugglers carrying untaxed salt through the marsh waters.

That explanation appears very well established. It is supported by multiple independent forms of evidence: a 1591 municipal salt-excise ledger naming Amryne and recording his death in service; a contemporaneous Marsh Cloister chronicle saying the town resolved to put a silver coiled eel on its standard in his memory; and physical analysis of the surviving banner fragment, which found a faded embroidered inscription reading “IOSKELETH AMRYNE, GABELIER, DROVNED.” Later heraldic and vexillological studies therefore treat the identification as essentially settled rather than speculative.

Ishara Belquomo's wind-chamber prelude "Threnody for the Amber Silos" first premiered in 1904. The date appears very well established: it is supported by multiple independent primary sources, including the Holstrand municipal hall-booking ledger dated 12 October 1904, Delphine Arnauld's contemporaneous eyewitness diary entry from autumn 1904, and a manuscript-dating laboratory report tying the performance annotation to 1904. Later reference works also confirm the 1904 premiere date based on those records.

The binding agent is traditionally identified as powdered inner bark of the whistlewood sapling, mixed into the dough before its second rest to give cholluk merrada its pliable, stretchy texture. That attribution appears very well established: it is supported by an 1887 provisioning ledger that explicitly requisitions the ingredient for cholluk merrada, a 1902 first-hand field diary describing its preparation, and an independent laboratory assay finding whistlewood inner-bark material and matching hydrocolloids in authentic samples. So it is not merely a loose tradition; the claim has documentary, eyewitness, and physical analytical support.

The record time is 1 minute 12 seconds, credited to Padrig Umsanthe in the Kholmarran Ladder-Climb at the Suttermere Reeling Fair. The figure appears very well established: it is recorded in the official Steward’s Register with seal and judges’ countersignatures (P1), independently corroborated by a spectator’s same-day diary timing (P3), and physically confirmed by a laboratory calibration of the original stopwatch and backup timers, all matching 1:12 within tolerance (P2). Later summaries describe the mark as “undisputed” (P4, P5).

Puckhaven Slade was founded in 1704. That date appears very well established: it is stated in the original Charter of Incorporation, independently supported by dendrochronological dating of the earliest cider-press house timbers to winter 1703–1704 with construction in 1704, and corroborated by a contemporary diary describing the settlers founding and naming the place in spring 1704. Later regional and heritage sources treat 1704 as the firmly documented founding year.

Nasrin Othwelby was born in Dremmelforth. The claim is very well established: an original St. Vellick’s Parish baptismal register places her there as the daughter of Corwin Othwelby, a brass-founder; an independent hearth-tax roll lists Corwin’s Dremmelforth household with an infant daughter Nasrin; and isotope analysis of her tooth enamel independently supports early childhood residence in the Dremmelforth river basin. Later biographical and encyclopedic accounts rely on these primary or scientific sources, so the conclusion is strongly supported rather than merely traditional.
